documents.title: Using Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) Technology at the University at Buffalo
documents.stance_why: The guidance encourages experimentation but sets no coursework stance: "Students must use AI tools in accordance with their instructor's guidance", so decisions about permitted use are left to instructors and the main binding rules concern data privacy and compliance.
documents.summary: University-level IT guidance on generative AI: data privacy, accuracy, bias, copyright and best practices, with scope, definitions and review roles. Students are told to follow instructor guidance and the academic integrity policy.

units.why: The opening says UB "recognizes the potential" of Gen AI "to advance research, instruction, learning", a statement of benefits rather than a rule, so P87 (benefits) with modality informs.
units.anchor: recognizes the potential that Generative Artificial Intelligence (Gen AI) tools have to advance research
units.frag_end: daily office functions at the university.

units.why: The summary says it is "important to provide guidelines for the responsible and effective use" of AI, which sets the purpose and scope of an institution-level framework (P56), not a rule on a specific use.
units.anchor: important to provide guidelines for the responsible and effective use of these emerging technologies

units.why: "individuals should not enter Category 1 or Category 2 data" into tools without a university contract is a data-protection prohibition addressed to everyone, so P50 (protect data, prefer contracted tools), should-not as worded.
units.anchor: individuals should not enter Category 1 or Category 2 data
units.frag_start: When using Gen AI technology individuals
units.frag_end: university has not entered into a contract with.
units.policy: Individuals should not enter Category 1 or Category 2 data, including non-public research data, into Gen AI tools with which the university has no contract.

units.why: "Information shared with Gen AI is not private" and prompts are stored to train models explains why the data rule exists; a factual warning about tool data practices, so P50 with informs.
units.anchor: Information shared with Gen AI is not private and could expose proprietary or sensitive information

units.why: "Gen AI has made it easier for malicious actors to create sophisticated scams" is a security-awareness warning (P75) and tells users to "consider privacy risks"; P75 fits better than P50 because the threat is scams.
units.anchor: Gen AI has made it easier for malicious actors to create sophisticated scams
units.frag_end: data breaches utilizing information provided to Gen AI software.

units.why: "works to ensure that all software and applications procured ... have the appropriate privacy, security, and accessibility protections in place prior to purchase" describes pre-purchase review of tools, P65, binding the university (admin).
units.anchor: software and applications procured on behalf of the university have the appropriate privacy, security

units.why: "AI-generated content can be inaccurate, misleading, or entirely fabricated" warns that output is unreliable, which matches P31 (verify AI output); the copyright mention is coded separately.
units.anchor: AI-generated content can be inaccurate, misleading, or entirely fabricated

units.why: "Students must use AI tools in accordance with their instructor's guidance" hands the decision on permitted use to each instructor, so P04 (instructor sets the rule), modality must, addressed to students.
units.anchor: Students must use AI tools in accordance with their instructor’s guidance

units.why: "in compliance with the university academic integrity policy" ties AI use to existing integrity rules; P77 (comply with existing policy) rather than P36 because it does not classify misuse as misconduct.
units.anchor: in compliance with the university academic integrity policy

units.why: The "AI Hallucinations" bullet defines hallucination ("text and images that sound and look plausible but ... have no basis in fact"), a warning about unreliability, P31 informs.
units.anchor: create text and images that sound and look plausible but deviate from reality

units.why: "Gen AI models often include biases from the data they are trained on" names a bias harm, so P53, informs.
units.anchor: Gen AI models often include biases from the data they are trained on

units.why: "extremely limited transparency into the data which is used to train their models" is an ethical concern about opacity, grouped under P53 (ethical concerns), informs.

units.why: The bullet on "Unauthorized inclusion of others works; rights and attributions" says models imitate creators without credit and may include others' work in research; this is a copyright and attribution concern, P52.
units.anchor: some Gen AI software will imitate creators without clearly stating so
units.frag_end: incorrect or no citation and attribution.

units.why: "Individuals should be familiar with the terms of use for the software" is a should about licensing and terms (P52).
units.anchor: should be familiar with the terms of use for the software which they are using

documents.unit: Department of Computer Science and Engineering
documents.title: CSE Generative AI Policy
documents.stance_why: The policy does not ban AI in scholarly writing; it holds authors responsible and says AI-derived content "must be clearly identified (including the use of Generative AI tools in a supporting role; e.g., editing for grammar)", which is permission with disclosure conditions.
documents.summary: CSE departmental policy limited to theses, capstone documents and other scholarly writing. It lists benefits and harms of generative AI, then holds authors responsible for content, originality and ownership, with disclosure of AI use.

units.why: The policy opens by recognizing AI "can help students communicate in an unfamiliar language and have applications when brainstorming, ideating, or building temporary scaffolds"; it names benefits without a rule, so P87 informs (P15 would need an explicit permission).
units.anchor: Generative AI tools can help students communicate in an unfamiliar language

units.why: "Generative AI is not a substitute for careful, thoughtful, well-reasoned thought" says AI must not replace thinking, P32 (students remain primary thinker), stated as a belief.
units.anchor: Generative AI is not a substitute for careful, thoughtful, well-reasoned thought

units.why: "its output can be incorrect, misleading, or otherwise harmful" warns about output quality, P31, informs.
units.anchor: its output can be incorrect, misleading, or otherwise harmful

units.why: "its overuse has profoundly negative environmental impacts" is an environmental concern, P53, informs.
units.anchor: its overuse has profoundly negative environmental impacts

units.why: "over-reliance on Generative AI reduces cognitive engagement with acts of creation" gives a skill-building reason to limit reliance, P41, informs.
units.anchor: over-reliance on Generative AI reduces cognitive engagement with acts of creation
units.frag_start: and that over-reliance on Generative AI

units.why: The preamble says CSE "reaffirms the following baseline expectations for all scholarly work produced by its students, faculty, and staff, particularly for Theses and Capstone", setting scope and principles for research writing, P62 (research and scholarship).
units.anchor: baseline expectations for all scholarly work produced by its students, faculty, and staff

units.why: "CSE holds the author or authors of a scholarly work to be responsible for its content, regardless of the process used" means authors own what they publish even if AI helped, P29.
units.anchor: responsible for its content, regardless of the process used to create the publication
units.frag_start: CSE holds the author or authors

units.why: "It is the authors' responsibility to make sure that referenced citations are valid" and claims supported addresses AI hallucinated references; P31 (verify output) fits since the duty is to check content, though AI is not named.
units.anchor: make sure that referenced citations are valid, that their arguments are self-consistent
units.fit_note: AI is not named in this sentence; it is a general duty to validate citations and claims.

units.why: Authors "are expected to adequately disclose its provenance" and credit sources, a disclosure duty, P24, should.
units.anchor: expected to adequately disclose its provenance, relationship to other related works
units.frag_start: CSE holds the author or authors
units.fit_note: Disclosure of provenance and credit to related works generally, not AI specifically.

units.why: Content whose provenance cannot be asserted, such as "artifacts produced using Generative AI tools", "must be clearly identified", a must-disclose rule, P24.
units.anchor: such content must be clearly identified
units.frag_start: If provenance of some content can not
units.frag_end: supporting role; e.g., editing for grammar).

units.why: The parenthetical extends identification to "the use of Generative AI tools in a supporting role; e.g., editing for grammar", so even light editing help is disclosed; a separate scope rule, P24 with fit note.
units.anchor: Generative AI tools in a supporting role; e.g., editing for grammar
units.frag_start: such content must be clearly identified
units.fit_note: Extends disclosure to supporting uses such as grammar editing, which P24 does not specify.

units.why: "By publishing the work, the authors assert their understanding and approval of the published work and all claims it makes" requires understanding of what is submitted, P30; P29 is the ownership sentence just before.
units.anchor: assert their understanding and approval of the published work and all claims it makes
units.frag_start: CSE expects the author or authors
units.fit_note: Understanding is asserted on publication, for scholarly work, rather than being explained on request.
